description: We are Netrunners, a team of Cybersecurity Engineering students from Universidad Politécnica de Durango (UNIPOLI) in Durango, Mexico. Combining our background in systems security, data integrity, and software development, we leverage computer vision and telemetry analysis to tackle critical aerospace challenges and enhance mission safety for NASA Space Apps 2026
summary:
Flame Runner is an interactive research platform and bilingual evidence assistant built for the Flame in Freefall challenge. Because fire behaves unpredictably without buoyancy-driven airflow, NASA has spent decades studying space combustion, leaving vital data scattered across over 10,000 pages of technical reports.

To solve this, we consolidated 24 investigations and over 2,000 tests from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository into a unified database of 1,568 source-verified findings. Our web application lets researchers select mission scenarios—from the ISS to lunar habitats and Mars bases—to rank relevant studies, compare test conditions side by side, export CSV datasets for flammability modeling, and query an AI assistant (powered by Gemma 4) that answers strictly from cited NASA documents.

By exposing critical research gaps—such as the lack of partial-gravity and high-oxygen habitat data—Flame Runner helps engineers bound fire risks for upcoming Artemis-era missions while accelerating safer fire suppression technologies on Earth.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Flame Runner transforms decades of scattered NASA microgravity combustion research into an interactive, searchable web platform. We extracted, cleaned, and verified 1,568 findings across 24 investigations, 2,000+ tests, and over 10,000 pages from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository into a structured database.

The platform works through four core modules:

  • Mission Scenario Explorer & Ranking: Users select a mission profile—the International Space Station (ISS), a lunar habitat, a pressurized rover, or a Mars surface base. A dedicated ranking algorithm orders all 24 investigations by relevance to that environment's gravity, pressure, and oxygen conditions, explaining why each study applies.
  • Side-by-Side Comparison View: Researchers can compare multiple investigations simultaneously to inspect hardware configurations, fuel types, test variables, and measured outcomes.
  • CSV Data Export: Users can download clean, structured test datasets directly as CSV files to feed predictive flammability and fire-safety models.
  • Bilingual Evidence Assistant (English & Spanish): A grounded conversational assistant searches our verified database and answers questions strictly using NASA’s documented findings. Every claim includes clickable citations linking to the exact original source page, and the assistant refuses to answer off-topic queries or speculate beyond the text.

What benefits does it have?

  • Eliminates Literature Bottlenecks: Reduces weeks of manual reading across thousands of dense PDFs into seconds of targeted exploration.
  • Zero-Hallucination Traceability: Unlike generic chatbots, every extracted finding in our database was cross-checked against its exact source text, giving engineers and students verifiable, page-level citations.
  • Bilingual Accessibility: Full support for English and Spanish lowers language barriers for international students, researchers, and outreach programs.
  • Ready-to-Use Modeling Inputs: Direct CSV exports bridge the gap between archival NASA reports and modern computational modeling.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Flame Runner addresses a critical safety challenge for human spaceflight: without buoyancy-driven airflow, fire changes shape, spreads unpredictably, becomes harder to detect, and extinguishes differently.

By exposing a major gap in current data—specifically, that PSI contains virtually no partial-gravity combustion tests or elevated-oxygen tests matching planned lunar habitats—our platform helps engineers bound fire risks using existing microgravity and Earth data until upcoming missions like LUCI and FM2 deliver empirical results. Beyond space exploration, Flame Runner connects orbital combustion insights to terrestrial innovations, including high-efficiency water mist extinguishers, advanced smoke detection, and improved firefighter protective gear.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Backend & Database: Python, FastAPI, and SQLite.
  • Frontend & Deployment: React, Tailwind CSS, hosted on Render (flame-runner-frontend.onrender.com).
  • AI & Inference Stack: Local inference running Gemma 4 on a dedicated team server for the bilingual evidence assistant, with Anthropic Claude used as a fallback and during development for automated document extraction, data cleaning, translation, and code review.
  • Data Sources: All documents, test parameters, and visual assets originate from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and NASA Space Apps resources.

How is your project creative?

Rather than building another generic document search engine, we designed Flame Runner around engineering decision-making and transparency about what science does not yet know. Combining a scenario-based relevance ranking with an explicit "research gap" framework allows users to see both existing evidence and missing boundary conditions for Moon and Mars missions. Pairing a strict, citation-locked local LLM (Gemma 4) with side-by-side experimental comparisons turns static archival reports into an active mission-planning tool.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific Rigor & Trust: Because fire safety leaves no room for fabricated data, we implemented automated text-verification against original NASA documents and constrained the assistant to answer strictly from retrieved sources.
  • Mission-Specific Context: A fire on the ISS (1g-free microgravity, ~21% $O_2$) behaves very differently from a fire in a lunar habitat (1/6g partial gravity, elevated $O_2$, lower pressure). We structured our ranking logic around these real operational parameters.
  • Usability & Open Science: We prioritized clean visual comparisons, bilingual access, and open CSV exports so both aerospace engineers and students can immediately use the data.
